Header:
Date: 2027-03-19
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Lena Morris (Redwood SE), Theo Park (Redwood Product), Samira Voss (Redwood SE), Ravi N. (Paladin CTO), Maya O. (Head of ML), Noah L. (DevOps), Elena G. (PM)
Recording id: ff-20270319-paladin-json-pt1-84a7

Summary (auto):
Quick live playthrough of Redwood JSON mode + console tooling focused on tool/function calling, schema guardrails, and fallback strategies. Customer asked about private deployment constraints, latency vs cost, and audit/SSO. Agreed next steps: pilot SOW, sample workloads for benchmarking, hands-on console workshop.

Topics:
- JSON mode and typed outputs
- Tool calling and sandboxed execution
- Fallback policies and model variants
- VPC/private options and KMS/encryption
- Pilot scope and success metrics

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I see we have most of the Paladin Data crew, hi hi. Quick roll call, I will hand to Lena for the demo flow but the goal today is, we want to show JSON mode, how you can wire tool calls safely, and then run through fallback policies. Any time stop me.
[00:18] Ravi Narayanan: Sounds good. Appreciate you running this, our main ask is to understand safety around invoking internal APIs and how Redwood prevents leakage to external tools.
[00:28] Lena Morris: Totally, that's a good north star. I'll start in the Console, show the schema playground, then flip to a live run with the API and the sandboxed tool runner. Some parts might be slightly choppy — the auto-transcription may show weird names like 'Redwood Dedicate' — sorry in advance.
[00:40] Maya Ortiz: No worries, and we also want to see how you measure quality degradation when switching to smaller quantized variants.
[00:49] Lena Morris: Yep, we'll demo that in the Optimize tab — quick quants and a canary.

[01:05] [screen share starts — Console]
[01:12] Lena Morris: Alright, Console -> Models -> JSON Mode. You'll see a sample schema here: it's a typed object, required fields, enums and a sub-schema for 'actions'. The playground shows immediate validation errors so the model output can be coerced or rejected.
[01:32] Elena Griggs: Is that validation real-time? Like, can it call our webhook only if it passes validation?
[01:38] Lena Morris: Exactly. You can attach an execution policy: 'only-invoke-on-validated-output'. That way the tool runner will not fire unless the JSON validates.
[01:45] Noah Li: And when it invokes, does Redwood proxy the call or does the model talk directly to external endpoints?
[01:50] Samira Voss: Good q. By default the runner is sandboxed and proxied through Redwood for hosted customers. For Private/VPC installs you can configure an on-prem runner that sits inside your network, so calls never leave the VPC.
[02:05] Ravi Narayanan: We need the VPC runner. Also KMS — we use AWS KMS with an HSM-backed key for encrypting keys at rest, can that be integrated?
[02:13] Theo Park: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS/HSM; you can point the control plane at the CMK for secret rollout. The audit logs include per-request metadata for crypto operations.

[02:30] [demo continues: schema editing]
[02:35] Lena Morris: Here I add an 'action' type: {"type":"send_email","to":"string","template_id":"string","sensitive":false}. Note — you'll see I flagged fields as sensitive, the console will mask them in logs and redact for retained traces.
[02:52] Maya Ortiz: Masking is great. Do the masked fields still appear in the tool payload? We need templates to be complete but not logged.
[02:59] Lena Morris: They can be included in the executed payload but we support configurable retention policies: no retention, partial redact, or full retention with KMS wrap. Admins can choose per-route.
[03:12] [00:03:12] Speaker 2: There's also an option for token-level cost breakdown, which helps estimate per-invoke expense when you switch quantization.
[03:22] Avery Chen: Quick note — many teams worry about latency hit with these safety checks. Our runtime does prefix caching and pre-validation to keep median p95 in the same ballpark. If you need strict p50 SLOs we can suggest dedicated pools.

[03:40] [live run — API mode]
[03:45] Lena Morris: Now I'm going to send a sample prompt via the API with tool schema. Observe the response: the model returns an 'action' matching the schema, the Console validates, then the runner posts to a demo webhook.
[03:58] [00:03:58] Maya Ortiz: I see in the webhook body there's an extra field called 'kv_cache' — is that the kv cache info?
[04:05] Lena Morris: That's coming from the runtime's context — we sometimes surface a short KV hint for debugging, but that can be toggled off in Prod.
[04:14] Ravi Narayanan: If a model returns malformed JSON, what happens? Do you attempt to coerce?
[04:20] Samira Voss: You can set a policy: 'reject_on_invalid', 'attempt_coerce', or 'fallback_to-safe-action'. In practice we find 'attempt_coerce' with a strict schema validator plus a post-check is the safest for user-facing flows.

[04:40] [simulation: malformed response]
[04:44] Lena Morris: I'm going to force a malformed payload. Console shows validation failed, and because this route is set to 'fallback_to_safe_action' it triggers a safe no-op action and logs the event in the audit trail.
[04:58] Noah Li: Does the fallback generate alerts? We want immediate paging if something that touches PII fails to validate.
[05:04] Lena Morris: Yep, there's an alerting hook you can wire to PagerDuty or a Slack channel, and the event includes the failure reason (validator error) but excludes redacted fields.

[05:20] [discussion: model variants & quants]
[05:24] Avery Chen: On the Optimize tab, you can define candidate models (full fp16, int8 quant, and a distilled variant). Redwood can route traffic by policy — latency sensitive routes go to a higher perf model, cost-bound tasks go to quantized model. We also support automatic canary rollouts and rollback if eval metrics drop.
[05:40] Maya Ortiz: How do you measure eval metrics? We require exact-match on structured fields plus semantic score on outputs.
[05:47] Theo Park: Our evals let you upload labeled prompts; we run them across model variants and compute schema success rate, field-level precision, and a semantic sim score. Reports are exportable.

[06:03] [timing note — demo moves to fallback orchestration]
[06:10] Lena Morris: Now for fallback orchestration: you can chain fallbacks — e.g., primary model -> small quant -> remote hosted safer model. Each fallback can have independent timeouts and per-step cost caps.
[06:24] Ravi Narayanan: We have an internal policy that PII queries must never go to external hosted models. Can fallback skip those?
[06:31] Samira Voss: Yes, route policies can block routes containing flagged PII tags. The runtime inspects tags before attempting fallbacks. You can also pin certain routes to Private-only.

[06:48] [questions about procurement & compliance]
[06:50] Elena Griggs: Procurement will want to understand support SLAs and the monthly committed capacity model.
[06:56] Avery Chen: We'll send the Dedicated pricing options in the SOW; monthly reserves give you dedicated GPU pools and guaranteed throughput which helps meet p95 SLOs.
[07:07] Maya Ortiz: Is there a SOC 2 report we can share?
[07:10] Avery Chen: Yes — we'll include SOC 2 and ISO docs in the follow-up link. Also we have an architecture whitepaper for VPC/private control plane setups.

[07:22] [hands-on: console policy editor]
[07:25] Lena Morris: I'm editing a route policy: name 'payments-invoke-guard'. The policy has validators, a KMS key id, and 'no-external-hosted' flag. I'll save and show a live test.
[07:40] [00:07:40] Maya Ortiz: That flag's UI is nice. Does the console allow RBAC to restrict who can change route policies?
[07:47] Samira Voss: Yes, SSO + SAML, role-based groups, and you can assign granular permissions per-model and per-route.

[08:05] [demo latency check — simulated p95 numbers]
[08:09] Lena Morris: For this test route p95 is ~420ms on our dedicated pool in us-west — quantized variant drops cost ~40% with a slight bump in error rate. We'll share the exact numbers in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[08:22] Ravi Narayanan: Can we run our own load tests? We'd like to see end-to-end in our VPC.
[08:28] Avery Chen: Yes — we typically provision a trial Private runner for customers to run their load tests. That was one of the pilot asks.

[08:40] [crosstalk, minor audio skip]
[08:45] Noah Li: On network egress — do you have TLS mutual auth between the runner and the model service? We need mTLS with client certs.
[08:52] Theo Park: mTLS is supported for Private runners; for hosted we use TLS + regional peering and IP allowlists.

[09:05] [policy lifecycles & audit trails]
[09:10] Lena Morris: Policies are versioned; you can roll back and the audit trail stores who changed what and when. We also support policy 'dry-run' mode to test without enforcement.
[09:21] Maya Ortiz: Dry-run with sample workload is a must for us.
[09:25] Avery Chen: We'll include that in the SOW scope.

[09:33] [wrap-up: recap & next steps]
[09:35] Avery Chen: Cool — recap: we'll send SOW + pricing, include SOC2/ISO links, provision a Private trial runner for benchmarking, and schedule a 2-hour console workshop. Lena will drop example schemas and policy exports. Maya/Noah to send sample prompts and traffic profile. Does that match?
[09:52] Maya Ortiz: Yep, that matches. One ask: can you add explicit evaluation for structured-output exact-match?
[09:57] Theo Park: Absolutely — we'll add exact-match + semantic scoring to the eval matrix.
[10:02] Ravi Narayanan: Thanks, this was helpful. One last thing — competitive question: if we wanted to self-host an open-source runtime, how does Redwood compare?
[10:10] Avery Chen: Short answer: Redwood gives you the orchestration, model catalog, safety primitives, and managed kernels. If you self-host you lose the console, the integrated eval tooling, and the unified fallbacks; some customers do it for cost but then build a lot of ops around it.
[10:26] Noah Li: Understood. We'll review the SOW and get back with a timeline.

[10:34] [meeting ends — 52m total — auto end marker]
